etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English habit, from Latin habitus (“condition, bearing, state, appearance, dress, attire”), from habeō (“I have, hold, keep”). Distantly related to gift. Replaced Middle English abit, from Old French abit, itself from the same Latin source. Displaced native Old English þēaw.

definitions.definition: An action performed on a regular basis.

quote.citation: 1824, Geoffrey Crayon [pseudonym; Washington Irving], Tales of a Traveller, (please specify |part=1 to 4), Philadelphia, Pa.: H[enry] C[harles] Carey & I[saac] Lea, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: a man of very shy, retired habits

quote.citation: 2013 July 19, Ian Sample, “Irregular bedtimes may affect children's brains”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 34:
quote.text: Irregular bedtimes may disrupt healthy brain development in young children, according to a study of intelligence and sleeping habits.  ¶ Going to bed at a different time each night affected girls more than boys, but both fared worse on mental tasks than children who had a set bedtime, researchers found.

definitions.definition: An action performed repeatedly and automatically, usually without awareness.

quote.citation: 2000, “I'm With Stupid”, in WYSIWYG, performed by Chumbawamba:
quote.text: Another white boy band / They're happy on demand / Everything is planned / Until the singer gets a habit

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English habiten, from Old French habiter, from Latin habitāre (“to dwell, abide, keep”), frequentative of habeō (“I have, hold, keep”); see have.

quote.citation: 1887, Harriet W. Daly, Digging, Squatting, and Pioneering Life in the Northern Territory of South Australia, page 132:
quote.text: Here I began my shopping, was interviewed by dressmakers, and naturally had much to do to habit myself for civilized life again.

definitions.definition: A long piece of clothing worn by monks and nuns.
A piece of clothing worn for a specific activity; a uniform.

quote.citation: 2015, Alison Matthews David, Fashion Victims: The Damages of Dress Past and Present, →ISBN, page 34:
quote.text: Sidesaddle riding habits were prestigious tailored sportswear appropriate for the equestrian pursuits of the truly wealthy.

quote.text: Noble and milde this Perſean ſeemes to be,If outward habit Iudge the inward man.

quote.text: There are, among the statues, several of Venus, in different habits.

[…] it was always my fate to choose for the worse, so I did here; for having money in my pocket and good clothes upon my back, I would always go on board in the habit of a gentleman; and so I neither had any business in the ship, or learned to do any.

[…]  [Gulliver’s Travels], volume I, London:  […]  Benj[amin] Motte, […], →OCLC, part I (A Voyage to Lilliput), page 30:
quote.text: There were ſeveral of his Prieſts and Lawyers preſent, (as I conjectured by their habits) who were commanded to addreſs themſelves to me, and I ſpoke to them in as many Languages as I had the leaſt ſmattering of, which were High and Low Dutch, Latin, French, Spaniſh, Italian, and Lingua Franca; but all to no purpoſe.
